prompt: Design a minimal local algorithm that decides which cell of a cellular graph receives the next unit of computation budget, given per-cell potential and resistance values. The rule must use only a cell and its direct neighbors (no global view). Explain why the rule is fair and why it cannot starve a cell forever.

an engineer who wants the smallest mechanism that could work
a teacher who explains by building one small piece at a time

steps.text: Design a minimal local rule for choosing the next cell to receive computation budget using only a cell and its direct neighbors.
Each cell has potential and resistance values; fairness and no permanent starvation are required.
A local score comparison cannot find a global maximum because no cell has global view.
Use a single token: the token-holding cell receives the next budget, then passes the token to a neighbor.
Pass the token by local round-robin over neighbors (rotor-router), optionally biasing neighbor order by potential/resistance.
On a connected undirected graph, a rotor-router token visits every cell infinitely often, ensuring fairness.
Potential/resistance bias alone may starve cells; round-robin or aging is needed for the no-starvation guarantee.
The minimal mechanism is a local token with round-robin/biased handoff, assuming the graph is connected.

steps.text: The task is to choose the next cell for a computation budget using only a cell and its direct neighbors, with fairness and no starvation.
A local-max score rule alone can leave multiple contenders, so use a single budget token that moves locally.
Give each cell potential p_i, resistance r_i, and age a_i since last service; define score s_i = (p_i + α a_i)/(r_i + 1).
At each step the token holder compares its score with those of its direct neighbors and moves the token to the highest-scoring cell, which receives the budget.
The token holder needs only its own values and its neighbors' values, so the rule has no global view.
If a cell is not served, its age grows, so its score eventually exceeds any neighbor's fixed or reset score.
Since the graph is connected, this rising score pulls the token through boundary cells toward any starved region.
Therefore every cell is served infinitely often; the rule is fair and cannot starve a cell forever.

gaps: The exact ε-smoothed proportional selection rule (w_j = ε + p_j/(r_j+1), choose j among self and neighbors) is not represented as a distinct move.
The key role of ε>0—making every self/neighbor transition positive and preventing zero-probability starvation traps—is absent.
The finite irreducible Markov-chain/recurrence proof is missing: connectedness plus positive local transitions implies every cell is visited infinitely often almost surely.
Fairness is left ambiguous: the decomposition does not distinguish no-starvation from equal/proportional service, nor explain that potential/resistance only bias stationary frequency.
The token/update semantics and local normalization are not decomposed, including whether the current holder receives now or chooses the next holder.
